Visual artist Jason Cook  creates kinetic sculptures and robotic installations using electronics, programming and mechanical engineering. In The Walking Chair (2025), an ordinary wooden chair is transformed into a moving machine. A system of motors, mechanical parts and electronic components is attached beneath the seat, allowing the chair’s legs to move. By giving a familiar piece of furniture the ability to walk, Cook changes the way we perceive an everyday object. The chair is no longer simply something we sit on  it becomes an object with a movement of its own. #art #artist #weird #chair #avantgarde

Sprout is Fauna Robotics’ small, developer-focused humanoid robot built to work safely around people in real-world spaces like labs, schools, offices, retail, and entertainment venues. It’s designed less like a shrunken factory robot and more like a “human-environment” platform: lightweight, padded/soft on the outside, and engineered to reduce impact risk with compliant control and limited joint torques. What makes Sprout interesting is the “full-stack” approach. Fauna positions it as a ready-to-build-on system where core capabilities—movement, perception, navigation, and social expression—work out of the box, so teams can spend time on applications instead of rebuilding fundamentals.  Sprout also leans into interaction: it can be directed via voice, has expressive features (like articulated eyebrows and LED facial elements), and supports things like whole-body control, grippers for manipulation, and even VR-based teleoperation within a unified hardware-software stack.  Pricing reported at launch is about $50,000, targeting researchers, universities, and builders who want a capable humanoid platform without starting from scratch.#ainews #robotics #Techtok #futuretech

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

A története egészen az 1880-as évekig nyúlik vissza. Az Egyesült Államokban akkoriban nagyon népszerűek voltak az úgynevezett mechanikus perselyek, amelyek valamilyen mozgást végeztek, amikor beledobtak egy érmét. A Jolly Nigger Bank is ezek közé tartozott: 1888-ban szabadalmaztatták, és a gyártója azért készítette el, mert az emberek szerették az ilyen játékos perselyeket. A figura azonban egy korabeli rasszista karikatúrára épült. Abban az időben sajnos sok reklámban, játékban és használati tárgyon ábrázolták így a fekete embereket, amit akkor sokan elfogadhatónak tartottak, ma viszont már sértőnek és rasszistának tekintenek. Az interneten a persely később mémmé vált, főleg azért, mert viccesnek találták a mozgását és a furcsa kinézetét. Magyarul ezért ragadt rá a „Jolly Nigger pénznyelő” név is. Ma már inkább egy történelmi kuriózumként emlegetik, ami jól mutatja, hogyan változtak a társadalmi normák az elmúlt több mint száz évben. The story of the Jolly Nigger Bank goes back to the 1880s in the United States. At that time, mechanical coin banks that moved when you inserted a coin were very popular. The Jolly Nigger Bank was patented in 1888 and was created as a fun novelty to encourage people, especially children, to save money. The figure was based on a racist caricature of Black people that was common in American culture at the time. While many people then saw it as acceptable, today it is widely recognized as offensive and racist. Many years later, the bank became an internet meme because of its unusual appearance and the way it mechanically "swallowed" coins. Today, original examples are mostly found in museums or private collections and are viewed as historical artifacts that reflect the racial attitudes of their era. #history #bank  #blacklivesmatter
